To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the scalar-proton interaction can be measured if the scalar-neutron interaction is known, but not viceversa; (ii) the scalar-neutron and axial-proton interactions can be measured if a multi-target experiment using both iodine and sodium comes online; (iii) the dark matter mass can be measured with a ton-scale detector if the inelastic parameter is known, but the latter cannot be inferred from the data.

(i) the scalar coupling to nucleons is not measurable with ton-scale experiments; (ii) the axial coupling to nucleons can be measured with ton-scales experiments; (iii) the inelastic parameter can be measured with a few ton-scale experiments; and (iv) the dark matter mass can be measured with multi-ton-scale experiments

(1) the scalar-proton coupling is left essentially unconstraned if the assumption $|f_p/f_n|\sim1$ is relaxed, while the scalar-nucleon coupling can be determined if the target complementarity is exploited, (2) the axial-proton coupling can be determined with fair accuracy if the target complementarily is exploited, and (3) the inelastic parameter and the dark matter mass can be measured with accuracy of tens of keV and tens of GeV respectively,
In summary, our research is concerned with
a detailed assessment of the information that can be extracted from the next generation of direct searches for dark matter.
the question of what (and what not) can be measured with the next generation ton-scale direct detection experiments.
the limitations of future direct detection experiments and, more generally, with the question of whether a multi-ton detector can determine the dark matter properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while the scalar and axial couplings of dark matter to nucleons can be measured, their absolute values cannot be determined.
the dark matter mass, the inelastic parameter and the ratio of couplings $a_p/a_n$ can be measured, but the absolute scale of the scalar couplings and axial couplings cannot.
future direct searches will not be able to measure the WIMP-nucleon cross sections.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the prospects for constrains on dark matter parameters are not as optimistic as often claimed, but that a multi-target approach can be used to extract a great deal of information on the dark matter particle properties.
, with a few notable exceptions, future ton-scale direct detection experiments will be able to measure only the dark matter velocity distribution and, to a lesser extent, the WIMP coupli

, while the scalar-proton coupling is essentially unconstrained by the next generation of dark matter experiments, the axial-proton coupling and the ratio of scalar and axial couplings may be measured with fair precision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a multi-ton experiment using a single target is likely to leave a large portion of the dark matter parameter-space unconstrained.

a multi-ton experiment with a variety of targets will be able to measure the dark matter mass, the inelastic parameter and the ratio of couplings $a_p/a_n$, but not the absolute values of $a_p$ and $f_p$.
the next generation of direct detection experiments can only probe the dark matter parameter region that is already excluded by the null results of the LUX and PandaX-II experiments.
